newsitem.title: USA: Merck's Fosamax to go before FDA committee.
newsitem.headline: Merck's Fosamax to go before FDA committee.

text.p: Merck and Co's osteoporosis treatment Fosomax should receive a favorable recommendation from a U.S. Food and Drug Administration committee Thursday regarding claims the drug prevents the disease, analysts said.
"We forecast it will meet a favorable review tomorrow, which would clearly be a positive for the company and would help expand the market a bit," David Maris, an analyst at Aros Securities said.
Fosomax was launched in October 1995 as a treatment for osteoporosis, a loss of protein tissue from the bone which makes bones brittle.
The first symptom of the disease, which was more common in women, whites and the elderly, was often a broken hip.
Osteoporosis could provide a multi-billion dollar market opportunity five years from now, Maris said.
In 1996, Fosomax had worldwide sales of $282 million. If ultimately cleared as a drug which prevented osteoporosis, its sales could reach between $500 million and $600 million in 1997, analysts said.
"This has the potential to be a blockbuster drug, to the extent that any one drug can be a blockbuster for a company as large as Merck," Maris said.
The company declined to comment on the upcoming review.
Rodman & Renshaw analyst James Keeney said: "Any time a company goes for a prevention claim for a drug, it is targeting a much larger population base."

Fosomax would also be the first nonhormonal drug to prevent osteoporosis, although it might not much market share away from women already taking commonly-proscribed hormonal replacement therapies, several analysts said.
Women produced less estrogen as they age and synthetic versions of the hormone were sometimes used to treat the side effects of menopause as well as osteoporosis.
"Hormone replacement therapies have three benefits," Michael Binz, an analyst at Edward Jones, said. "They treat the side effects of menopause, they lower lipid levels and they treat osteoporosis."

While they had been linked to higher incidence of breast cancer and cancer of the uterus, Binz said these therapies were not likely to lose ground to Fosomax or Eli Lilly and Co's raloxifene, an osteoporosis prevention drug now in clinical trials.
"Treatment of osteoporosis is a complex matrix which depends on the doctor, the patient and how well the sales people market the product," Binz said.
Higher Fosomax sales were linked to an increased number of new patients, rather than to patients switching from hormone replacement therapies to Fosomax, Maris said.
Roughly 20 million people in the United States had osteoporosis, Maris said. Of that, 16 million were undiagnosed, he said.
"The really big story here is the number of patients who could start taking medication for osteoporosis," he said. "And if Fosomax gets prevention claims, the number becomes bigger."
